title: Merek and the Missing Things
markdown:
Ogre Merek lived by the quiet rhythm of the mountain winds. His dwelling, snug in warm black rock, saw him emerge each dawn as the sun painted jagged peaks with rose and molten gold. His task was never a grand quest. It was ash-bloom dew, gathered from hardy flowers before the sun grew too strong: a sparkle, a whisper of the earth’s fiery heart mixed with star-twinkle. He used it to polish smooth river stones until they mirrored the mountain sky.

One particular dawn the world outside his ordered routine decided to flutter. Dew-catcher of moon-spun silk ready in his calloused hands, he heard a bleating, small and lost, like a tiny bell in a vast meadow. Merek, whose soul found solace in deep silence, paused. Unfamiliar things, even small ones, sometimes deserved a closer glance.

He followed the sound, heavy feet surprisingly soft on ash-strewn ground. Huddled near stubborn grey-green moss was a creature no bigger than his outstretched knee: a mountain goat, coat the colour of a brewing storm, wide innocent eyes holding sky. The little goat shivered. Merek felt a strange soft tug in his chest.

“Well now,” he rumbled, a deep cello note. “You seem to have misplaced your herd, little one.”

The goat blinked those sky-blue eyes and bleated again, a desperate plea. His cherished solitude warred with an unaccustomed feeling of responsibility. “Patience now,” he murmured. “All will be revealed in time.” With a gentleness that belied his size, he scooped the trembling creature into moss-green hands. “You are covered in moss, and you have found me. Moss, then.” And so Merek, who had ventured out for dew, returned with an entirely unexpected companion.

The Ember’s Rest lay a short trek across the ash meadows, nestled near a spring that bubbled with constant soothing warmth. Merek went there infrequently, for supplies, with quiet efficient purpose. With Moss curled warm in his embrace, the inn seemed louder. Chatter, clatter of mugs, a hundred overlapping conversations. Moss wriggled; Merek held her a little tighter.

Inside he found his usual quiet corner. Reputation for civility smoothed the curious glances. He settled Moss beside him with a pile of sweet hay. A fragile calm began to settle. Then the hum of the inn unravelled into three commotions at once.

A portly merchant, face florid, waistcoat straining, remonstrated with Anya the sprightly innkeeper. “My prize-winning Moonstone Cheddar. Gone. Vanished right from my saddlebag. Foul play, Anya. Or a remarkably cunning rodent.”

A harried cook, apron dusted white, brow slick, bustled past muttering. “The Whisperwind Herbs. My special blend for the dragon stew. Right by the larder, I swear, and now — poof. How am I to make the stew sing?”

A young bard, beautifully carved lute slung across his back, approached Anya crestfallen. “My Lute of Lingering Melodies. In its case by the hearth. I turned my back for a moment. Gone.”

Merek glanced down. Moss chewed hay, delicate nose twitching. A small seed of suspicion: three valuable items, same inn, same time. And Moss, boundless curiosity, an appetite for shiny things, fragrant things, things that caught her bright eye.

He had brought her here for comfort. Now he felt implicated. Shoulders slumped. He had yearned for a quiet day. Instead he sat at the centre of a small inn-wide mystery. A tight clenching in his stomach.

He cleared his throat, pebbles in a stream. “Excuse me. Perhaps I can assist.”

Anya nodded gratefully. “Merek, always a steady presence. Tell us your thoughts.”

Moss was nudging a small incredibly shiny pebble. Merek looked from merchant to cook to bard. “I believe our missing items might not be as lost as they currently seem. And I believe our young Moss here might have some very particular insights.”

With surprising patience he retraced her gentle movements. A faint dusting of flour on the floor, a whisper of it clinging to her fur, the sweet scent of baking bread near a crevice. She had not stolen maliciously. She had gathered, unthinking. The magnificent cheddar wheel, nibbled then abandoned near the hay, too cumbersome. The Whisperwind Herbs, fallen unnoticed from the cook’s hand, tucked neatly into a crevice by the kitchen door as if offered back. The lute had rolled a short distance; Moss, seeing a frayed bit of red ribbon near the hearth, had nudged it closer to investigate, and so it had been overlooked.

A collective sigh. The merchant chuckled, belly shaking. The cook wiped his brow, grinning. The bard strummed a cheerful chord. Anya’s eyes twinkled. “Well, Merek. You’ve solved our little puzzle. And Moss, you certainly have been a busy goat.”

Evening drew long gentle shadows across the volcanic slopes. The Ember’s Rest, no longer filled with suspicion, decided to celebrate. Warm crusty bread, hearty stew carefully seasoned with the recovered herbs — which did, Anya swore, make it sing — and steaming spiced cider. The bard played a tune that lingered like the lute’s name promised. The merchant offered everyone a sliver of Moonstone Cheddar, slightly nibbled, still prize-winning. Moss, forgiven, accepted a second pile of hay as if it were a medal.

Merek, Moss a warm sleepy ball at his feet, felt a warmth that had nothing to do with volcanic springs. He had stepped out of his predictable routine into a flurry of misunderstandings, and instead of retreating he had untangled the knots. The inn’s noise, which had once felt like an assault, now sounded almost like weather: something you could sit inside, if you had a goat and a corner and a little patience.

Stars pricked the inky sky above the peaks. Moss slept, breathing even. He had protected her, and in doing so found he could navigate noise as well as silence. Dawn would still want dew. The ash-blooms would still wait. Patience now: all would be revealed in time. And the stones he polished would, perhaps, hold a little extra sky for a goat who collected the world by accident and gave it back.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
